225.bp: Vision-language models (systems that see images and understand text together) are incredibly powerful but expensive to run. When millions of people use them online, companies either suffer slow responses or rack up huge bills. The goal is to serve these models to users fast and cheaply without sacrificing the ability to answer hard visual questions.
225.wh: The problem sits at a crossroads: run everything on the cloud and you get accuracy but latency spikes and costs explode; run everything on a phone and you save money but the tiny device can't hold the full model, so answers get worse. You can't have all three—speed, cost, and accuracy—at the same time. The trick is knowing which tasks are easy enough for a phone to handle and which ones need the full model back in the cloud.
225.ap: ShiftVL splits the work between your device and a distant server. Your phone holds a smaller, simpler version of the model, tuned with ViTexLoRA (a way to add task-specific skills without teaching the whole model). For routine requests it answers directly. For tricky or rare requests, it asks the cloud server with its bigger, smarter model to take over. It also predicts which tasks you'll ask about next and loads their helper-tools early, like preheating an oven.
225.ww: This works because most requests fall into a few common patterns—they're similar enough that a phone can spot them and answer. Only the weird edge cases really need the full brain in the cloud. By shipping the easy work to the phone, you slash the number of expensive cloud calls. By predicting what's coming next, you avoid the delay of fetching tools on demand. The result is the cloud does less, costs less, and the phone answers faster.
225.po: In real tests with actual vision-language models, ShiftVL cut cloud costs by up to 76% and response delays by 43%, while still keeping answers accurate across many different visual tasks. That's the practical gain: a system that feels fast to users and doesn't bankrupt companies running it.

226.bp: When companies run large language models in production—think millions of queries per second on real hardware—tiny choices about batch size, data-copying strategy, and chip scheduling matter hugely for how fast the system runs. Every new model and every new setup (different GPUs, different cloud data centers) requires manually figuring out the best numbers all over again, which is tedious and error-prone.
226.wh: The parameter space explodes quickly: batch size, GPU parallelism, graph caching, topology—each one interacts with the others in subtle ways. A batch size of 64 might be perfect on one server but terrible on another because of how memory flows. You can't just copy settings from your friend's setup because their hardware is different. Testing every combination by hand would take months.
226.ap: llm-tuna wraps a search tool (Bayesian optimization) around the open-source vLLM serving engine and parallelizes the search across multiple machines. Instead of manually guessing, it systematically tries promising configurations, learns which ones work best, and zeros in on high-performing settings. It avoids repeating the same mistakes and respects hardware limits so it never suggests a setup that's worse than just running vLLM as-is.
226.ww: Bayesian search is smart about picking which experiments to try next—it learns a model of how performance depends on the settings and picks configurations likely to be winners. By running many trials in parallel across servers, you get the answer fast. The safety guarantee (never worse than the baseline) means you always have a fallback if the search finds nothing better.
226.po: On real language models (including huge mixtures with hundreds of billions of parameters), llm-tuna found setups that run 33% faster than vLLM's default, without any human tuning. For companies deploying these models, that's a direct win in throughput and cost.

227.bp: Child sexual abuse material (CSAM) is a horrifying crime, and detecting it online saves lives. A crucial step is figuring out the age of the child in the image, both for law enforcement investigations and for automated filtering systems to catch and remove this content quickly.
227.wh: Machine-learning systems trained to classify ages often work like a black box: they give an answer but don't explain why, making it hard for human experts and investigators to trust or override them. Also, attackers actively try to fool age classifiers to evade detection. The challenge is building a system that's both explainable (so humans can see the reasoning) and robust against attacks.
227.ap: The researchers built a system that mirrors how human experts actually decide a child's age: it looks at the face, the body proportions, and biological markers together. Instead of one neural network black-box, it combines three separate pathways for these three signals, then fuses their outputs. This way, when the system says 'this is a prepubescent child,' you can see which of the three signals led to that choice.
227.ww: By splitting the decision into three parallel human-interpretable pathways, the model is forced to make decisions for real, visible reasons—not hidden internal patterns that might be brittle or spurious. If someone tries to fool one signal (e.g., add makeup), the other signals still work. The fusion approach is inherently more resilient because it doesn't rely on a single decision route.
227.po: The fusion method achieved 81% accuracy (F1-score 0.807) on real CSAM cases for the most critical group (youngest children), and it resisted adversarial attacks better than end-to-end models. For law enforcement, that means faster, more trustworthy automation to identify and block abuse material.

228.bp: In digital marketing, companies invest money in ads and campaigns to make sales. Traditionally, they set a budget at the start—say $10,000—and run their campaign. But in reality, how well the campaign performs should influence how much they spend next: if it's working great, invest more; if it's failing, pull back.
228.wh: The traditional math (Bandits with Knapsacks) assumes a fixed budget you announce upfront. Real marketing doesn't work that way. The budget and the results are tied together in a loop: profits flow back into the next round of spending. This creates a circular dependency that breaks the traditional math, and it opens a new risk: you could spend so much on a bad campaign that you run out of money and go bankrupt. Nobody had solved this before.
228.ap: The researchers built new math (Bandits with Endogenous Knapsacks) that treats the budget as a moving target, shaped by performance. They designed an algorithm that tunes spending up or down based on how well each marketing channel is working, while watching out for the ruin scenario (when you lose more than you have left). They also solve a two-level problem: not only how much to spend right now, but also how to set your reinvestment rate for the whole campaign.
228.ww: The primal-dual algorithm handles the circular feedback by updating both the spending and the constraint (budget) together, step by step. The risk-aware piece works because it doesn't just chase profit—it also reserves a safety margin to never go broke. By learning the optimal reinvestment rate, you adapt how greedy you are, trading off short-term wins for long-term safety.
228.po: They validated the theory with both live A/B tests on real ad campaigns and simulations. The system can now adaptively increase or decrease marketing spend in response to performance while guaranteeing the company won't go bankrupt, a fundamental improvement over fixed-budget approaches.

229.bp: When you want to predict when a customer will buy again, or how long until a machine part fails, you're predicting time intervals in human behavior or systems. Large language models are incredibly flexible and can read context, so they seem like they should be good at this. The question is: are they actually better than traditional time-series models?
229.wh: Large language models are trained to handle language, not quantitative patterns in time. When you add more context about the customer (purchase history, browsing, demographics), you'd think it helps—but it can actually overwhelm the model and make it confused about the numbers. This contradicts the common assumption that 'more information is always better.'
229.ap: The researchers tested modern language models on a simple but realistic task: predict how many days until a customer repurchases. They compared zero-shot language models against statistical methods (like exponential smoothing) and traditional machine-learning models, adding different amounts of customer context each time. They measured accuracy (how close to the true interval) and ranked the methods.
229.ww: Language models excel at language patterns but struggle with raw quantitative structure—they're built to predict the next word, not the next number in a sequence. Adding context about behavior helps up to a point, but too much context floods the model with information it doesn't know how to compress. Statistical and machine-learning models, by contrast, are explicitly designed to spot numerical patterns and don't get distracted by side details.
229.po: Large language models beat simple statistical baselines but consistently lost to dedicated machine-learning models. Even more surprising, adding extra user details beyond moderate context actually made language models worse. The takeaway: language models aren't the right tool for time-interval prediction, and hybrid systems that combine statistical methods with linguistic context might be the real win.

230.bp: Recommendation systems learn what each user likes and what each product is about, then suggest relevant items. But users' tastes change over time and products' popularity shifts—a sweater is hot in winter, irrelevant in summer. The system must update its internal understanding of users and items as new interactions arrive, capturing this temporal drift.
230.wh: Most systems update their understanding of users and items after each interaction, but they overwrite the old information with the new. So if someone loved horror movies for years but watched one rom-com last week, the system might start recommending rom-coms, forgetting the long history. Also, historical patterns (e.g., this user always buys from this seller) get erased. The system loses the full picture of who someone really is.
230.ap: TraceRec retraces the history of each user and item by walking backward through past interactions (reverse chronological random walks). For each neighbor in that historical path, it restores that person's or item's representation to what it was at the time of the original interaction. Then it recommends based on this richer, time-aware picture instead of just the latest snapshot.
230.ww: By remembering each interaction in its original context (who someone was at that moment, not who they are today), the system captures stable long-term preferences without erasing them. The reverse walks prioritize recent history but don't ignore older patterns. The result is a model that sees users as they evolve over time, not as a single frozen state.
230.po: On six real-world datasets of user behavior over time, TraceRec beat eight competing methods, lifting the recall metric (did the user click on a recommended item?) by up to 17%. This means more relevant suggestions and better user satisfaction in systems that have to adapt to changing tastes.

231.bp: In web search, e-commerce, and social networks, data is connected in complex, high-order ways: a person is connected to many products, many reviews, many other people. Traditional graph neural networks struggle with these multidimensional relationships, so special hypergraph models were invented. But these models are expensive and slow. Knowledge distillation (teaching a small student model to copy a large teacher) promises to speed things up, if done right.
231.wh: Current distillation methods lean on a single large teacher, which limits what knowledge the student can learn—it's like studying from one textbook. Also, they assume the student just needs to copy the teacher's outputs, ignoring the student's own ability to learn the structure of the data. Neither side is fully developed.
231.ap: MARCH uses multiple large teachers, each trained differently, so they see different structure in the hypergraph. These teachers transfer knowledge at two levels: individual nodes and groups of nodes (hyperedges). The student learns from all of them at once, picking up complementary insights. The student also uses a contrastive loss (a technique that pushes similar things together and different things apart) to build strong internal representations, not just copy the teachers.
231.ww: Diverse teachers each see different high-order patterns, so together they teach a richer picture than any single teacher can convey. The two-level transfer captures both local node details and global group structure. The student's own contrastive learning forces it to encode structure meaningfully, so it's not just a passive copier—it actively builds better representations than its teachers had.
231.po: In experiments, MARCH's student models learned better than any single teacher alone, and sometimes outperformed all the teachers together. This is a hallmark of good distillation: the student becomes smarter than its teachers by synthesizing their diverse views.

232.bp: Social media is filled with text, images, audio, and video all mixed together. Powerful multimodal AI systems can now understand and generate across these formats, but deploying them on platforms at scale raises real safety questions: Can they be tricked? Do they hallucinate false information? Are they misused to spread misinformation and hate?
232.wh: Multimodal models are so new and powerful that we don't yet have solid benchmarks or safety tests for them in real social media contexts. Each modality (text, images, audio, video) has its own risks, and combining them creates new failure modes nobody has fully mapped yet. Platform companies need guidance on what to measure and how to defend against abuse.
232.ap: This workshop brought together researchers and practitioners to discuss two main areas: (1) how to fuse text, images, audio, and video together safely and correctly, and (2) how to evaluate and test these systems for both capability (do they follow instructions?) and safety (do they avoid hallucination, misleading output, or adversarial manipulation?). Papers covered multimodal fusion techniques and adversarial robustness.
232.ww: By collecting research under one roof, the workshop creates a common language and shared benchmarks. Safety evaluation on large multimodal models requires cross-disciplinary work (AI safety, platform policy, linguistics, computer vision) that individual labs struggle to do alone. Standardized tests help platforms deploy these systems more confidently.
232.po: The workshop accepted 10 papers from 7 countries, providing researchers and platform teams with both novel methods for multimodal analysis and practical safety evaluation strategies for large multimodal models deployed on social media.

233.bp: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique where a large language model reads web documents first, then generates an answer. This helps the model give current, fact-checked answers without retraining. But the quality of retrieved documents directly controls answer quality, and real-world web corpora are messy and full of misinformation.
233.wh: Rerankers improve RAG by pushing accurate, relevant documents higher in the result list. But when you look carefully at what happens to document types during reranking, something surprising happens: while helpful documents rank higher, harmful documents (misinformation, junk, misleading content) also rise higher. The reranker is so focused on relevance that it accidentally promotes both good and bad content together.
233.ap: The researchers studied what happens to different types of documents (ground truth, misinformation, junk) before and after reranking. They discovered harmful documents increased significantly in the top results. Based on this finding, they built a risk-aware reranker that balances the benefit of pushing relevant content up against the harm of surfacing misinformation, using a metric called information gain.
233.ww: Rerankers optimize a single signal (relevance), which blindly elevates both true and false content if they're both relevant to the query. By explicitly modeling the risk—the chance a harmful document gets shown to the language model—you can trade off a small loss in top-1 accuracy for a big reduction in misinformation exposure. This prevents the language model from being tricked by false content.
233.po: The risk-aware method ensures that harmful documents in top results decrease while still ranking ground-truth documents highly, reducing the chance that language models generate and spread misinformation across the web—a direct safety win for RAG systems.

234.bp: Website fingerprinting is a traffic analysis attack: an eavesdropper watches the encrypted data flowing to and from your device, sees the pattern of packet sizes and timings, and figures out which website you're visiting—even though the content is encrypted. This breaks your privacy. Defense systems try to hide these patterns, but attackers keep improving their techniques.
234.wh: Most fingerprinting research assumes people only visit website homepages, but real people jump to dozens of subpages, open multiple tabs, and mix activities. Previous work couldn't distinguish which subpage you visited (just 'you were on Facebook'), and multi-tab settings weren't realistic. This gap between lab and reality limits how well defenses actually work.
234.ap: HiFi-WF models the fingerprinting task as a hierarchy: first identify the main website (homepage level), then identify the specific subpage within it. A unified neural network extracts features from traffic patterns, and layered encoders model the hierarchy. Attention mechanisms capture dependencies between the two levels, and an enhanced decoder prevents nonsensical predictions (e.g., a subpage that doesn't exist on that website).
234.ww: By treating the problem hierarchically instead of flat, the model can leverage constraints: some subpages only appear on certain websites. The multi-level attention captures that if you know the website, that constrains which subpages are possible. This structure lets the model learn more efficiently and make finer-grained inferences than if it tried to predict subpage directly.
234.po: HiFi-WF achieves fine-grained subpage identification in both single-tab and multi-tab settings, moving beyond the unrealistic homepage-only assumption. This more realistic evaluation helps designers build better privacy defenses by revealing what attackers can actually infer from real-world browsing patterns.

235.bp: Real-time systems (streaming data from sensors, servers, applications) produce data constantly, and anomalies—unusual events that deviate from normal—must be caught instantly. Think equipment failures, fraud transactions, or security breaches. But as systems evolve, the definition of 'normal' changes, so anomaly detection must adapt online without storing massive historical data.
235.wh: Existing systems assume anomalies fit fixed, known patterns, so they struggle when the normal behavior itself drifts (new feature launches, seasonal change). Also, storing all history to retrain is memory-hungry, and retraining from scratch for each new batch is slow. You need to learn continuously without blowing up memory or computation.
235.ap: DESS builds a small, representative summary (proxy) of all the historical data seen so far, capturing what 'normal' looks like. As new data arrives, it updates this proxy to include fresh patterns. For each incoming data point, it uses multiple timescale features (short-term blips, long-term trends) and only trains a small, modular subset of its parameters. Old, trained parts are frozen, so only new lightweight features are tuned.
235.ww: The compact proxy acts like a memory capsule: it shrinks terabytes of history into a small model that still encodes what to expect. By mixing multi-timescale features, you catch both sudden spikes and gradual drift. Training only a subset of parameters (parameter-efficient training) keeps memory low and speed high, so the system adapts in real time without refetching the past.
235.po: On real anomaly datasets, DESS beat competing methods by up to 17.5% in accuracy while cutting training time by 65%. Real-time systems can now adapt to changing normal patterns without exploding memory or computation costs.

236.bp: Harmful content—misinformation, hate speech, propaganda, cyberbullying—spreads across social media, news sites, and messaging apps in many languages and on many platforms. Shutting down one source just pushes bad actors to another platform or language. There's a need for research that sees harmful content as a whole, not isolated pieces.
236.wh: Most research tackles one harm type on one platform (misinformation on Twitter, hate speech on Facebook), in one language. But harmful content is strategic and adaptive: spreaders shift platforms and languages to evade moderation. Without seeing the big picture, local defenses can't stop the underlying problem.
236.ap: The DHOW workshop brought together researchers to study harmful content (misinformation, abuse, propaganda) as one phenomenon spanning platforms, languages, and current events. Papers covered detection, mitigation, and characterization of harmful content using both traditional methods and large multimodal models. The workshop explicitly included current crisis topics (wars, elections) and multilingual coverage (7 countries).
236.ww: By unifying the study of different harm types under one frame, patterns emerge: a misinformation campaign on Facebook might branch to TikTok and Telegram; a hate-speech vector in English might appear in German or Arabic. Researchers sharing tools and datasets can build defenses that work across these transitions, not just within one silo.
236.po: The workshop accepted papers on cross-platform, multilingual harmful content detection and mitigation, providing the research community with methods and datasets for defending against coordinated, adaptive disinformation and abuse at scale.

237.bp: Networks show relationships between things: people following people, cities connected by roads, atoms bonded in molecules. Traditional graph neural networks assume a simple rule: connected things are similar (homophily). But real networks violate this constantly. In social networks, people often befriend those different from them; in biology, opposing charges attract. The assumption breaks, and performance collapses.
237.wh: When a network violates the homophily assumption, existing methods treat those 'rule-breaking' connections as noise and try to remove them. But removing edges throws away real information. The challenge is building a method that respects both homophily edges (where similar things connect) and heterophily edges (where different things connect) as equally valid.
237.ap: Graph Weighted Aggregation (GWA) uses Ricci Curvature (a geometric measure of how space curves around a point) to quantify the influence between connected nodes. It combines three pieces of information: the features of nodes, the network's structure, and label information (what class each node belongs to). Based on this, it weights each connection: homophily edges get high weight, heterophily edges get moderate weight, and all are used together.
237.ww: Ricci Curvature naturally distinguishes homophily from heterophily: it's high where similar nodes cluster (homophily) and low where different nodes connect (heterophily). By using it as a weight, the model can attend to both types of edges without throwing any away. Combining features, topology, and labels ensures the weighting reflects the true role each edge plays.
237.po: GWA outperformed state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, showing that respecting both homophily and heterophily edges leads to better performance than treating one as noise. This is especially important for real-world networks where mixed connection types are the norm.

238.bp: Time series forecasting (predicting electricity demand tomorrow, traffic flow in an hour, stock prices next week) powers infrastructure planning and trading. Multivariate forecasting (tracking dozens of correlated signals) is especially hard. New approaches use frequency-domain analysis (breaking signals into sine waves) to capture repeating patterns, but two pitfalls trip them up repeatedly.
238.wh: In frequency analysis, weak but important signals (rare irregular patterns) drown in noise and get ignored during training. Meanwhile, strong periodic signals (daily, weekly patterns) get distorted when neural networks transform them, weakening the prediction. You need to preserve both the weak details and the strong cycles without one eating the other.
238.ap: GFMixer splits the problem into two parallel paths. The first (Temporal Gradient Block) finds weak signals by looking at how the time series is changing, detecting small but meaningful movements. The second (Fourier-Aware Attention Block) preserves strong periodic patterns by explicitly modeling frequency information and guarding against distortion. Both outputs combine via residual connections, blending the two sources of information.
238.ww: By separating low-amplitude (weak) and high-amplitude (strong) signals into different pathways, each pathway can specialize: one focuses on finding needles in noise, the other on protecting structure. Temporal gradients amplify weak signals by looking at rate of change, not raw values. Fourier-aware attention knows what periodic structure looks like and protects it explicitly.
238.po: GFMixer achieved first-place rankings on 37 out of standard benchmarks, beating all competitors. As a plug-and-play module, it also improved mainstream forecasting architectures. For real-world systems, this means more accurate demand and traffic predictions, reducing waste and improving planning.

239.bp: Multiple organizations (hospitals, banks, retailers) often want to collaborate on data science to improve service. The problem: each organization is reluctant to share raw data for privacy and legal reasons. Manifold learning—a technique that builds low-dimensional maps of high-dimensional data—could help them collaborate if done securely, with no single party seeing anyone else's data.
239.wh: Standard manifold learning algorithms require all data in one place or heavy communication between parties. Secure computation (techniques that let parties compute together without revealing data) is extremely expensive: each operation requires multiple rounds of encrypted messages. Scaling to real datasets seems impossible without reducing the computation somehow.
239.ap: SIsomap applies secret sharing (breaking data into cryptographic pieces shared among parties so no one party can reconstruct it) to Isomap (a classic manifold learning method). The researchers optimized the two costliest steps: finding top-k nearest neighbors and computing shortest paths in a graph. They exploit properties of Isomap to skip unnecessary secure operations, cutting 99% of communication overhead.
239.ww: By designing secure protocols specifically for Isomap's algorithm (not generic secure computation), you can skip steps that generic methods can't avoid. For example, in Isomap you only need top-k neighbors, not all-pairs, so the secure version only computes what's necessary. The result is orders-of-magnitude speedup without sacrificing privacy guarantees.
239.po: SIsomap's secure top-k nearest neighbors is 13.6 times faster than prior work, and its shortest paths is 1818 times faster. End-to-end, SIsomap is 11 to 29 times faster than baseline secure solutions, making collaborative manifold learning feasible for real multi-organization scenarios.
